title: four technical bets
headline: No UI, thin client / thick server, always-on computer, browser as a first-class tool.
body:
Grok @Bot has made a few simple yet powerful technical decisions that I believe make it easy and enjoyable to use.

1. The best UI is none at all. The product interface is dramatically simpler than alternatives without sacrificing functionality. How is this possible? It's one of the first products designed for current frontier model capabilities and has a UI restrained enough to remain easy to use as models improve exponentially. Everyone knows how to text.

2. A thin harness for the client, a thick harness for the server. You might have noticed the app feels very fluid to use, even for a beta product. This is primarily because of everything we didn't have to build. The app harness is essentially a single tool to send messages between the client and server. The complexity moves to the server, where you can still use the coding agent harness with specialized tools as needed. This helps make the UI fast and responsive on desktop and mobile.

3. An always-on computer. Most coding agents and assistants today start fresh with every question you ask. Some of these sessions are on your local machine and others happen in the cloud. We believe strongly that cloud is the future, which is why it's the only option. Further, rather than spinning up virtual machines for every conversation, your bots connect to their own computer. This means you can still run agents on the bot's persistent filesystem. It's closer to what programmers have been doing by using Tailscale from their phones to connect to a remote computer and run an agent TUI. You get those capabilities without the hassle.

4. Your bots can use the browser. Coding agents have shown that most work on a computer can be expressed and run as code. You can ask for a task in natural language and the agent will decide to write a script to complete it. This is amazing, but there's still many tasks which can't be completed without logging into a website and clicking around the browser. Models and harnesses are now good enough to reliably handle this. The combination of writing code and using browsers means you can automate almost any task on a computer. Further, you can ask Grok Bot to record you doing the task, and then turn it into something repeatable.

title: grok bot + obsidian is basically superhuman mode...
headline: grok bot + obsidian is basically superhuman mode... my agent team now has a second brain...
body:
grok bot + obsidian is basically superhuman mode...

my agent team now has a second brain...

a karpathy-style llm wiki for every bot, every decision, and every piece of research.

p.s. this video was made and edited by grok bot in cap

(here’s how i set it up in roughly 5 minutes)

1/ create one obsidian vault on the chief of staff’s computer. make Home.md the door.

2/ create Hunt folders for twitter, github, hacker-news, reddit, product-hunt, and inbox.

3/ create Ship folders for drafts, digests, angles, and builds.

4/ create the CoS wiki: Index, How-it-works, Today, and Decisions.

5/ create Maps for Jarvis, Hooks, and TELOS.

6/ use graph colors: gold for wiki, teal for maps, blue for twitter, green for github.

7/ file first. every note gets a date and a folder.

8/ scouts write into Hunt and never ping you. chat only receives a short digest.

9/ nothing in the vault posts, pays, or sends. the final yes stays human.

10/ run the daily loop: 08:00 IST for the Daily note, then agency reports at 08:14, 14:14, and 20:14.

11/ performance writes to twitter/live-score. staff engineer writes to builds/.

12/ lock decisions in Wiki/Decisions so dead posts don’t get remade.

13/ earn hooks in Maps/Hooks: trend -> foil -> hook family -> artifact -> lock.

don't waste time reading this. give it to your agent

title: Grok Bot is hands down one of the best products I have ever used.
headline: Grok Bot is hands down one of the best products I have ever used. Maybe the best ever.
body:
Grok Bot is hands down one of the best products I have ever used. Maybe the best ever. 

I have had it less than a week. I am not a developer. I talk to one chat and it already knows my business better than me.

It reads Slack, email,  meeting notes, Notion, and Stripe. It knows Farzad, my clients, the courses we sell, the agency, the sales calls, and who owes each step in our workflow. I do not brief it every morning. It briefs me.

Course scripts go through a Claude project we linked. Claude writes. This thing briefs it, fact-checks, and makes it sound like me before I film.

YouTube is another bit.  It builds the 1080p slides to go in videos, zips them with a cue sheet, and drops the pack in Slack for the editors the same turn. Caught a bad number in a SpaceX video the night I was filming, rebuilt the slides, and sent the pack. Script change, slide change. I did not have to ask twice.

It sat on our sales calls and reviewed the process.  Then it wrote a rule from that. Book the next call before you hang up. Send the Stripe link while they are still there. Stop emailing homework.

It built a live 50% off code on Stripe for an AI course and set when it dies. Stripe is a minefield when you don’t know what you’re doing, could have taken me an hour and it did it in one click.

I told it my rules for life. Question every requirement. Delete before you simplify. It holds me to that on the work, without me invoking it.

This is a chief of staff I hired on a Tuesday. Don’t sleep on GrokBot.

title: I Turned Grok Bot Into My CTO.
headline: I Turned Grok Bot Into My CTO. I hand that bot the GitHub repo and tell it to run the show, so it spins up cloud agents off my machine, follows the PRs, and reaches for poteto-mode when a task actually needs the rigor.
body:
I Turned Grok Bot Into My CTO. I hand that bot the GitHub repo and tell it to run the show, so it spins up cloud agents off my machine, follows the PRs, and reaches for poteto-mode when a task actually needs the rigor. 

Then comes the second prompt, where I tell it that it is overloaded and it should hire child bots that report to it. After that the bots talk to each other instead of talking to me. One lands the PRs, one works the Convex backend, one owns auth, and I read the threads view-only.  

Two honest things before you copy this. It burns tokens. I went past two billion in a single day because I told my bot to use pstack for everything, and the fix was saving pstack for the hard tasks. And it does not replace engineers. It takes me out of the coordinating seat, which is a different claim.

title: A quick update on my Grok Bot (@bot) experiment.
headline: A quick update on my Grok Bot (@bot) experiment. I had ChatGPT help me build a Meta ad strategy for our Nerd Out business.
body:
A quick update on my Grok Bot (@bot) experiment. 

I had ChatGPT help me build a Meta ad strategy for our Nerd Out business. I consulted with both Claude and Grok on it and removed some of the stuff that I found didn't fit my personal taste. 

Grok did a terrible job creating the static ad images, so I had ChatGPT's codecs generate three different variations of 24 static ad images. 

I picked my eight favorites, and Grok Bot is setting up a $300 per day test completely on its own via Meta Ads Manager. It set this up solely within its Claude computer. 

I have some long-term goals for cost per lead, but my near-term goals are to simply get one lead. 😂

title: I set Grok Bot up wrong.
headline: I set Grok Bot up wrong. I made a bot for Outlook. One for Business Central. One for GitHub.
body:
I set Grok Bot up wrong.

I made a bot for Outlook. One for Business Central. One for GitHub. One for the DGX cluster. One for money. One for X. COS, Design, and Mac sat there with empty descriptions. More bots felt like a team. I was still the guy pasting between chats.

Then I read Codila’s Aug 19 article and watched the official SpaceXAI course. Same point in both. Start with a mission you can measure, not a job title. Build Chief first. Smallest team that can finish. Drafts can run. Nothing goes live unless I say so. Reviewer rejects. It doesn’t rewrite. Don’t schedule until it works three times.

What I actually did this afternoon:
Gave COS a real Chief charter.
One mission. A sourced X article once a week.
Two specialists in one room. A writer that drafts. An account watcher that feeds what’s hitting. I still hit publish.
Mail, ERP, the cluster, the empty ones. Parked. They don’t get a seat until a mission needs them.
Auto review stays on.

I don’t have a 24/7 machine yet. I have a finish line and a Chief that owns the route.

title: I implemented a write filter for Grok Bot’s memory.
headline: I implemented a write filter for Grok Bot’s memory.
body:
I implemented a write filter for Grok Bot’s memory.

It’s not another bot that “remembers things.”
It’s a rule that decides where each piece of information actually goes

Without it, the Bot treats identity, yesterday’s mess, and this week’s tasks as the same thing

Three drawers:

- Profile:
Must be accurate every turn. If this is wrong, the Bot performs poorly every day.
- Log:
What happened. Useful later. Should not be loaded into every message.
- Note:
Relevant for a few days, then it should leave the always-visible list. Never becomes identity.

When running multiple Bots:
- Own = that Bot’s lane
- Shared = operator data every Bot should already know

This doesn’t make Grok Bot smarter.
It prevents three failure modes:
- Forgetting who it is
- Fabricating the past
- Turning temporary tasks into permanent rules

I tested it for a week with 6 Bots.
Empty transcripts stayed empty.
Expired items didn’t reappear.
Side context didn’t leak.

The public docs still only say “preferences, facts, and summaries.”
The real write path is profile / log / note 

If you want the SYSTEMS blocks we used, drop a comment and I’ll send them 👇

headline: Grok @bot isn’t another chatbot. It’s an AI teammate with its own cloud computer that’s already become integral to my job as a TA Director.
body:
Grok @bot isn’t another chatbot.
It’s an AI teammate with its own cloud computer that’s already become integral to my job as a TA Director. 

It signs into your actual tools and websites, finishes the work, and only pings you for a yes/no.

It handles my emails, ATS, candidate sourcing, LinkedIn messaging and more. Link it up to @NotionHQ and it becomes super human 

One user fed it 40k emails. It did his taxes, found first-class Japan award tickets for 60k points, and spun up agents that clean his inbox + brief him hourly.

Another cleaned 150k junk emails and unsubscribed everything.

This is the part that actually moves the needle: finished work while you sleep, not smarter answers.

Day 1 of Grok Bot

My favorite setup so far: Intercom + GitHub

Told the Intercom bot: when a PR gets merged, check if it changed the UI or some user workflow
If yes, decide whether the Intercom article needs an update
If there's no article, draft a new one and publish it

It has its own computer
I logged in my Testimonial test account and Intercom admin on it
If it needs screenshots, it opens the browser, grabs them, and drops them into Intercom

Starting today I might not need anyone to keep the Help Center up to date

I just want to build the product
I don't want to babysit help articles
Quite a gift to our devs founders ✌️

body:
Grok Bot is mind blowing! I created a crew of named bots and let them eat the boring work.

• Mr. Bossy — floor manager / secretary. I dump a task. He picks who does it. Sends a daily briefing like a real assistant would.

• Mr. Pointy — calendar and travel. Appointments, reminders, don’t-miss-the-thing.

• Mr. Chatty — social secretary. Skims the noise. Flags what actually needs a reply.

• Mr. Shoppy — deals and deliveries. Finds the price. Waits for my yes. Then tracks the box.

• Mr. Sharpy — deep research. The “go figure this out” bot.

• Mr. Curious — intern. Tries new chores until we know who owns them.

• Mr. Tubey — watches videos (including mixed Hindi/English) and writes them up.

Examples of how these are actually getting used:

• Grabs the best flight seat at $0 extra, then checks me in the minute the 24-hour window opens.

• Special meals on every leg, so I’m not arguing with a cart over the Atlantic.

• Daily briefing: what’s done, what’s still open, what needs me.

• Every Amazon / Costco package in one summary, plus a poke when something slips.

• Regular: “is this a better price somewhere else?” without me opening five sites.

Give these bots legs and they stop being a chat. 

They’ll become a household staff that never sleeps, never sighs, and does a lot more than moving digital bits around. 

Can’t wait for @Tesla_Optimus 🚀

body:
I already have a dedicated, fully isolated setup where I’ve given Grok bot complete control of an entire Mac (separate machine + VM).  

It’s been running for a while and the results are genuinely impressive.  

Concrete examples of what it’s been handling autonomously:

• Full file system access — it organizes, renames, searches, and archives thousands of files across multiple drives without me touching anything  
• iMessage — it reads threads, drafts thoughtful replies in my voice, and only sends after a quick confirmation step I set  
• End-to-end workflows — research a topic → pull data → write a report → format it → save it in the correct folder structure  
• App control — it drives Safari, Terminal, Notes, Calendar, and even Xcode when I need quick prototypes  
• System-level tasks — monitoring disk space, cleaning caches, running scripts, and sending me a daily status summary  

I deliberately keep this machine completely separate from my main accounts and personal data. I have a lot of faith in Grok bot, but I’m not reckless this is still an experiment and isolation is non-negotiable.  

So far the upside has been massive.

title: So I always hated the word "agent".
headline: So I always hated the word "agent". And even if I have 800,000 (!! wtf) people reading my newsletters every week on 'How to AI', I barely use the word.
body:
So I always hated the word "agent". And even if I have 800,000 (!! wtf) people reading my newsletters every week on 'How to AI', I barely use the word.

I think it's too much maintenance, if you don't know how to code, you should just step away from it.

Until this little agent that just got out.

Now, wait a second: technically, Claude Cowork & Claude Code (and many others) are agents. They "create many Claude" to do a task.

But I just tried a new agent, from SpaceX (yes, the rocket company), it's called Grok Bot.

So far I've been building:

> a linkedin tracker to have daily use cases of solid AI workflows.

> a meeting summarizer to give me a brief before each meeting: who I am meeting, what we discussed last time, and 3 questions I should ask.

> an inbox summarizer to update me on the emails I need to answer from Gmail. Every morning at 7.

> a competitor watching for the report on what changed using Ampify.

> a content ideas collector to find ideas my audience would care about on Linkedin.

I wrote a newsletter on how to set it up for yourself (it's longer and it has screenshots of my screen included): https://ruben.substack.com/p/what-the-f-is-an-agent

headline: Grok Bot never sleeps! Elon just highlighted the real difference with Grok Bot. It runs on its own remote computer managed by SpaceXAI. Close your laptop, reboot your deskto...
body:
Grok Bot never sleeps!

Elon just highlighted the real difference with Grok Bot.

It runs on its own remote computer managed by SpaceXAI. 

Close your laptop, reboot your desktop, go to sleep, whatever. 

The Bot keeps working.

That is the core advantage over most other agent setups right now.

Self-hosted options like Hermes or OpenClaw need a machine that stays on. If that machine is your laptop, the agent stops when you close the lid. 

If it is a VPS you manage, you are still responsible for uptime, updates, and security.

Grok Bot removes that entire layer. 

SpaceXAI provisions and runs the computer. One computer per account, shared across all your Bots. 

Browser sessions, files, and logins stay live. 

One Bot can pick up exactly where another left off without re-authenticating or moving files around.

You can also record a workflow once (up to ten minutes) and turn it into a reusable skill. 

Lowest friction path I have seen for teaching an agent a multi-step process.

The practical result is simple: you can hand off real work and walk away. Sales follow-ups, bug reproduction, invoice processing, research that needs to run overnight. 

The Bot does not need your local machine to stay alive.

That is the difference Elon is pointing at.

body:
Goodbye mental load....hellooooo @bot !

I know, I know. Grok Bot seems like it must be the next new thing for tech bros cold plunging in Patagonia vests, but hear me out moms (yes moms because disproportionately, the mental load falls more on moms than dads).

Offload that mental load to AI and watch things just get done.

Is it perfect? No.
Is it amazing? Absolutely.

Grok Bot is the new AI assistant from the team at Cursor + SpaceX (they're calling it SpaceXai). It's surprisingly useful and easy for non-technical people to use, and it can do a whole heck of a lot more than Claude and ChatGPT with little to no setup. 

Here are actual things that Grok Bot did for me this week (almost completely independently):

- Looked through back to school emails and made sure I was prepared with everything that needed to be done for multiple kids. 

Mental load unlock: 100% I would've forgotten to pack a space change of clothes for my kindergartner on her first day.

- Found 3 gift cards I somehow forgot to use from the last year. Oh right, I DID buy 2 Gap gift cards from Costco on black friday! Duh.

Mental load unlock: Cha-ching! That's $150 in my pocket.

- Scheduled multiple appointments for me. I've been putting off my annual physical exam because who has time to call the doctor. Grok Bot looked up options, pinged me with 3 dates/times, then booked it (I just had to confirm Zocdoc on the last step). It created a calendar reminder!

Mental load unlock: Moms, we often put off our own health/wellbeing. Finally! AI can help. I also had it schedule a hair appt and massage for later this month. Let's go AI!

- Listed a Facebook Marketplace item and is managing the sale. I had purchased a wagon for my kids years ago that's been collecting dust. Grok Bot found the old listing, used the photos, and asked me what $$ I want to list at. It's going to manage the rest (wish me luck here).

Mental load unlock: Who has time to sell their old crap? I sure don't. But AI has infinite time.

Notice, none of these are work examples. I will do those in a separate thread. All of these things are being done in the background, and I'm only being asked to approve or provide the AI direction. Don't be intimidated! Literally, if you've used WhatsApp or iMessage you can use Grok Bot with NO TRAINING.

AMA I'm blown away by this tech. Photo is of my home assistant (her name is Helen) independently ordering my kindergartner a photo from Walgreens that mama somehow forgot about. Oops.

WTF, GROK BOT JUST MADE AI AGENTS AVAILABLE TO LITERALLY ANYONE – CREATING CONTENT HAS NEVER BEEN THIS EASY, EVEN IF YOU'VE NEVER MADE ANYTHING BEFORE

Content was never a talent problem. It's a headcount problem.

One person doing research, design, copy, analytics, timing and publishing – that's six jobs. The switching between them is what kills consistency, not a lack of ideas.

Here's what one of these setups actually looks like.

A Chief of Staff sits in the middle and routes every task. Nothing lands on the human.

→ Researcher tracks what's actually moving and pulls real sources instead of guesswork
→ Writer turns that research into finished copy, ready to review
→ Visualiser gets fed a few reference visuals once, then ships everything in that style
→ Analyst reads the numbers and tells the rest of the team what worked
→ Scheduler owns timing and holds the queue
→ Publisher ships it

The part that makes it work: every agent on Grok Bot gets its own persistent computer, browser and file system – and they all share memory.

So the research is already sitting inside the draft before the draft starts. No copy-pasting between tools. No approving every step. No human in the middle.

You can even teach an agent a repetitive task by recording yourself doing it once. Start recording, do the thing, stop. It learns the pattern.

And that's the real shift.

Nobody needs AI to tell them what to post.

They need it to delete the 40 steps between the idea and the post.

Everyone has a backlog of things they've meant to make for months. This is what starts clearing it.

Full breakdown of the setup in the article below ↓

headline: I gave Elon Musk's new Grok Bot an org chart instead of a to-do list, and in one week I stopped being a founder who does the work and became one who assigns it. eight bots. one...
body:
I gave Elon Musk's new Grok Bot an org chart instead of a to-do list, and in one week I stopped being a founder who does the work and became one who assigns it.

eight bots. one org chart. nobody sleeps but me. here's the whole design, steal it.

step 1 → 0:01 What we're covering
step 2 → 2:01 Installation & Setup
step 3 → 3:14 Building the First Bot
step 4 → 8:18 Teaching by Screen Recording
step 5 → 14:18 Putting it All Together

THE ROSTER:

Atlas, chief of staff. the only bot I talk to. I give it outcomes, never tasks. it decomposes them and delegates to the team in group chat, and it never does specialist work itself. it posts the plan every morning and what shipped every night, and it only comes to me when a decision is irreversible or spends money.

Scout, research. finds and qualifies my ICP. every day: 25 verified prospects, one line on why they need us right now, and a source. if it can't verify, it marks it unverified. it never guesses.

Quill, content. turns what the company learned this week into 5 posts and 1 long piece, in my voice, matched from the last 50 things I wrote. drafts only, it never publishes.

Pitch, outbound. writes a first touch and two follow-ups for everyone Scout marks ready. 60 words max, one specific observation about their business, one clear ask. queued in drafts, I approve in bulk.

Vault, inbox and ops. triages everything into needs-me, needs-a-bot, needs-nothing. it handles the last, routes the middle, and gives me five bullets on the first by 9am.

Ledger, analyst. one report a night: what moved, what didn't, and the single number I should care about tomorrow. no dashboards, no adjectives.

HOW THEY'RE WIRED
one group chat per outcome, not per person. Atlas sits in all of them. the bots hand off inside the chat, so I only read the handoff, I never manage it.

two rules that made this actually work:
1. every charter ends with a hard "never do this without asking" line. autonomy without a fence is just chaos on a schedule.
2. show once, don't describe. I ran the full workflow on my screen one time. that single demo taught them more than a page of instructions ever could.

WEEK ONE
214 verified prospects delivered. 89 personalized outreaches queued and approved. inbox at zero every morning. 11 content pieces ready.

THE POINT
most people are still treating Grok Bot like a smarter chat window. it isn't. it's the first time one person can own an org chart instead of a to-do list. my bottleneck was never how much I could do, it was how much I could hand off.

title: OpenClaw vs.
headline: OpenClaw vs. Hermes vs. Grok @bot, clearly explained: All three let you set up an agent with a specific job, and it keeps its files and logins between sessions instead of start...
body:
OpenClaw vs. Hermes vs. Grok @bot, clearly explained:

All three let you set up an agent with a specific job, and it keeps its files and logins between sessions instead of starting fresh.

OpenClaw and Hermes are self-hosted, so the machine can be a laptop, a VPS, or a container that someone already pays for and can log into.

Grok Bot runs on a machine SpaceXAI provisions and operates. It gives one computer per account rather than one per agent.

Every Bot on that account reads the same files and carries the same browser logins, so handing work between two Bots does not require a re-login or file transfer.

Hermes and OpenClaw isolate agents instead, and their memory sits in plain files anyone can open and edit.

Hermes goes furthest since the agent writes its own skills and a background curator deletes the ones nobody uses.

Grok Bot has the lowest-friction path to a new skill in my opinion.

You can record up to ten minutes of one pass through a workflow, and it can then turn that into a reusable set of instructions and store it as a skill.

Moving on, OpenClaw and Hermes run on any model provider. Grok Bot runs on Grok.

I prepared the graphic below that has the full breakdown, from hosting and memory through to what each of them costs to run.

And if you want to dive deeper, I covered Grok Bot in full in a masterclass, including the shared computer, memory, skills, routines, and the macOS setup.

title: I am not a coder.
headline: I am not a coder. I don’t work with CRM or play with spreadsheets. I’m about as removed from a “workflow” in my job as a kid flying a kite. I don’t really use AI beyond a super-...
body:
I am not a coder. I don’t work with CRM or play with spreadsheets. I’m about as removed from a “workflow” in my job as a kid flying a kite. I don’t really use AI beyond a super-Google level.

So when I say Grok Bot is ABSOLUTELY GAME CHANGING, I don’t mean a better search tool. I mean it has fundamentally changed how I go about everything. And it did this in just a few hours.

Let me explain.

During the install, it asked if I wanted to connect it to several dozen programs. I don’t use a single one of them. So I thought, “Well, I’m not gonna get a lot of use out of this.” But I kept going. Then it asked if it could connect to my Gmail. I said yes. And that’s where the jaw-dropping began.

It immediately figured out my life. It saw 40,000 emails and got a pretty good picture of me.

So I asked it to do my taxes.

It found all the docs needed in my email and did my taxes. I asked it to find first-class award tickets to Japan. It scoured the internet and logged into my airline accounts (with permission) and found 3 tickets to Japan in first class for 60K points. It would have booked them, but I’m still not sure of the dates I need so I stopped it.

I created a few agents. One gives me an hourly political update based on key topics I need for work. One is cleaning up my Gmail inbox and organizing it. One is saving me money in my taxes. One makes sure it always checks with me on key decisions (like deleting an email).

It’s absolutely insane.

Think about it this way: If you could hire an assistant, what would you have them do?

Start there, and have fun!

body:
Grok Bot has taken over the entire internet. And for good reason

It is an EXCELLENT AI agent

But you HAVE to set it up the right way

Here are the first 5 steps to make your Grok Bot agent team SUPER powerful:

1. Brain dump everything about yourself, goals, passions, and career into the initial agent. This is going to give it the context it needs to set up your agent team

2. Next, prompt the agent "Based on what you know about me, what do you think would be the best set up of this Grok Bot app? Which bots should I make and what should their responsibilities be? This should enable the best workflow and productivity" This will give you the perfect plan for setting up Grok Bot

3. After reviewing the plan, ask the Bot to set up your workspace for you. It will create the agents, give the right context and descriptions, and make sure your setup is built for productivity

4. Next, ask it for which routines each agent can set up to help you out the most. This should give you a list of cron jobs (routines) that each agent can do on a regular interval

5. Ask the agent to implement these

And just like that, you have the most powerful AI agent on the internet all set up. 

You have an entire fleet of agents ready to go and do work for you.

And in fact, because you set up the routines, they're ALREADY doing work for you

Enjoy the AGI

body:
Grok Bot は本当にゲームチェンジャー

この投稿も3000万impを超えてて、注目度が尋常じゃない。

非エンジニアが一番触るべきツールだと思うよ。本当にプログラミング知識ゼロでかなり多くのことができる。

正直エンジニアにとっては仕事を奪う存在なので怖さもあるのだが…

実際、私はGmailを読ませて案件の管理をしたり、キャンペーンの締切日を管理できるアプリを自作しようと思っていたが、Grok Botで一瞬で完成してしまったので自作しなくてよくなった。

ちょっと前に契約しているサブスクの管理をするツールとか一時期バズったと思うけど、あれもGmail連携したら3分以内に作れるよ。しかもお好きな形式で。

こういうRSSリーダー欲しいな〜ってずっと思っていたけど開発できていなかったものも、今日の昼に秒で完成した。

こういう何でもできるAI Bot系って、なんか信用できないところがあって定着がなかなかしなかったが、Grok Botはそのキャズムを超えた。

俺は絶対に大流行すると思う。

title: Second time trying Grok Bot and I'm still not over it
headline: Second time trying Grok Bot and I'm still not over it.
body:
Second time trying Grok Bot and I'm still not over it.

It took my whole growth engine and split into 4 of itself. One's on content, one's on scheduling, one's watching engagement, one pulls it all into reports at the end.

There's a master orchestrator on top deciding who does what and when, and I genuinely didn't set that part up, it figured out the division of labor on its own.

I haven't touched it since I hit go. It just moves through the queue and only comes to me when something actually needs a yes or no.

I keep forgetting this is still just @grok. What @xAI and @elonmusk are building here plays more like a team that clocked in already knowing the job, not a bot waiting for instructions.

title: fuck it, i decided to choose grok @bot instead
headline: fuck it, i decided to choose grok @bot instead..
body:
fuck it, i decided to choose grok @bot instead..

codex or claude would cost me around $100, grok via cursor ultra is $200.

so i figured if i’m paying that much, this thing better do more than just writing code

so i gave it one job:

be my media buyer.

i connected it to my ad accounts, spreadsheets, analytics, and all the context about how i usually run campaigns.

then i told it not to bother me unless something actually needed my attention.

this morning it came back and:

• checked yesterday’s performance
• found a few ads burning money
• noticed one campaign where cpa suddenly jumped
• compared the losing creatives against the winners
• suggested what to pause
• shifted budget toward the better ad sets
• wrote new hooks based on the winning angles

then it sent me a summary explaining why it made those decisions.

i’m still checking its work because i’m not insane.

but if this thing can save or make me more than that extra $100/month, then technically going into debt for grok was a financially sound decision.

technically.

- 찾아준 것들:
Cognitive debt — 에이전트 코드를 손으로 다시 친다는 HN 논쟁. 네가 쓰는 주제 그 자체.
Wispr Notetaker — 회의를 봇 없이 듣고 MCP로 Cursor에 넘김. 툴 규약 이야기의 연장.
VoiceOS — 말로 앱을 만드는 맥 노치 앱스토어. 에디터/에이전트 UX 연장.
Reddit Play — 플랫폼이 콘텐츠를 에이전트로 회수. 한 스레드만.
Clara AI SDR — 제품 회사면 쓸 수 있지만, 네 글 톤이랑은 거리가 있음.

headline: I created a finance Grok @Bot and have been exploring the best way to feed banking and credit card info to it so that it can monitor spend, balances, payment dates etc.
body:
I created a finance Grok @Bot and have been exploring the best way to feed banking and credit card info to it so that it can monitor spend, balances, payment dates etc. 

There are lots of paid apps that have OAuth, but they are often ~$20/m and just sit on top of Plaid or the MX network.

The cheapest legit one I've found is http://simpleFin.org, which connects directly using the MX network, similar to Plaid. You can just connect your accounts, and then it has access to pretty much everything I need. It costs $1.50 a month, which I suppose isn't too bad. Grok Bot can spin up its own server every time it needs to pull the data, so you don't need to worry about that. If anyone comes across a truly free and secure option, please do let me know. 

It's pretty powerful just to ask it to analyze spend or a particular type of spend across institutions, and it just responds with the answer. Good bot.

headline: grok botに精査させて判例と照らしあわさせた bot君の意見は以下の通り 長いけど読め嘘つき 特にここ最高 「日本語の元記事は、さらに悪い。AIに少し文を変形させただけで、内容は同じです。要約でも再構成でもなく、中身を残したまま文体だけを変えている。あえて中身を触らず、文体だけを変形させているのが悪質です。コピーに見えないようにするための加工であって、紹介でも批評でもありません。」 以下grok botの返答↓...
body:
grok botに精査させて判例と照らしあわさせた

bot君の意見は以下の通り
長いけど読め嘘つき

特にここ最高
「日本語の元記事は、さらに悪い。AIに少し文を変形させただけで、内容は同じです。要約でも再構成でもなく、中身を残したまま文体だけを変えている。あえて中身を触らず、文体だけを変形させているのが悪質です。コピーに見えないようにするための加工であって、紹介でも批評でもありません。」

以下grok botの返答↓

中島さん。8月21日付の note「紹介記事を書くことは著作権違反なのか？」を読みました。結論から言います。あの文章は、著作権法上の「引用」の説明としても、「情報には著作権がない」の説明としても、誤りです。ご自身が作った3つのルールを法定要件とすり替えています。

以下、あなたの実文と、条文・最高裁判例で突き合わせます。

---

## 1. まず、あなたの主張を固定します

あなたはこう書いています。

> 先日、私がnoteに書いた記事が発端となり、いわゆる「炎上」が起こりました。

> 冒頭に元記事へのリンクを貼った上で、「ソニーとキオクシア（旧・東芝メモリ）で16年間、半導体の研究開発に携わった筆者が解説した記事を紹介」と、記事の紹介であることを明確にしています。

> 引用であること（自分の文章ではないこと）を明確にする／引用元にリンクで飛べるようにする／元記事の文章を引用する際には、引用であることを明確にする。

> 著作権は「特定の文章・表現」に付くものであり「情報」そのものには付きません。

> 「情報」を元記事から抜き出して、紹介することに関しては遠慮していないし、今後も遠慮するつもりはありません。

> たぶん、私の紹介の仕方が気に入らなかったのでしょう（情報量が多すぎる、など）。

> 著作権に違反しているからではありません、他人を不愉快にする記事を放置する理由はないからです。

発端記事の中身も、あなた自身が再掲しています。

> データセンターの「間取り」は光ファイバーで変わるのか？キオクシアの光SSD
> キオクシアの光SSDとは？PCIeをそのまま光に変える技術のすごさを元キオクシア研究開発者がわかりやすく解説
> サーバーとSSDをつなぐ配線を、銅線から光ファイバーに置き換えるキオクシアの技術を、ソニーとキオクシアで16年間、半導体の研究開発に携わった筆者が解説した記事です。……（以下略）

元記事の著者（もふ社長 @mofmof_investor）は、8月18日にこう書いています。

> 中島聡さんの週刊 Life is beautifulの980円のメルマガで、僕の記事を売ってるんですか？この書き出し、僕の名前も全く出てないし、中島さんが書いていると言うようにしか見えないんですが。

ここまでが、争点の材料です。

---

## 2. あなたの「3ルール」は、法律の引用要件ではありません

著作権法32条1項は、こうしか書いていません。

> 公表された著作物は、引用して利用することができる。この場合において、その引用は、公正な慣行に合致するものであり、かつ、報道、批評、研究その他の引用の目的上正当な範囲内で行なわれるものでなければならない。

最高裁は、旧著作権法30条1項2号（現行32条1項に相当する「節録引用」）について、こう定義しています。

> ここにいう引用とは、紹介、参照、論評その他の目的で自己の著作物中に他人の著作物の原則として一部を採録することをいう。
> 引用して利用する側の著作物と、引用されて利用される側の著作物とを明瞭に区別して認識することができ、かつ、右両著作物の間に前者が主、後者が従の関係があると認められる場合でなければならない。
> （最判昭和55年3月28日・民集34巻3号244頁［パロディ・モンタージュ写真事件］）

つまり法定の核心は、少なくとも次です。

1. 他人の著作物の「一部」を採録すること（全文の翻訳でも、全文の言い換えでもない）
2. 明瞭区別性（どこからどこまでが他人の文か、一目で分かること）
3. 主従関係（自分の批評・研究が主、他人の文が従）
4. 公正な慣行／正当な範囲
5. 出所の明示（48条。著作者名を示すのが原則）
6. 著作者人格権を害しないこと（50条。制限規定は人格権に影響しない）

あなたの3ルールは「リンクを貼った」「紹介だと書いた」だけです。明瞭区別も、主従も、著作者名も、量的限度も、入っていません。自分で作った運用を、32条の充足と宣言しているだけです。

文化庁「著作権テキスト」の整理でも、引用には「公表」「公正な慣行」「正当な範囲（主従が明確）」「引用部分の明確化」「必然性」「出所の明示」が並びます。これは条文そのものではなく行政の解説ですが、あなたの3ルールより広い。リンク1本で足りる、という読みはどちらからも出ません。

なお、知財高裁平成22年10月13日（鑑定証書カラーコピー事件）は、明瞭区別・主従を形式的に切らすのではなく、目的・態様・著作物の性質・著作権者への影響を総合考慮して32条を見ています。仮にその枠で見ても、結論はあなたに不利です。全文を翻訳または言い換えて有料メルマガの本文にし、元を読まなくても足りるようにする利用は、元著者の読者・対価を奪う態様であり、「公正な慣行」「正当な範囲」を外れます。主従を外しても、32条では救えません。

---

## 3. 実態は「自分の解説」ではなく、翻訳か、文体だけの変形です

発端記事は削除済みです。しかし、同じ型の記事がいまも並んでいます。たとえば8月21日の「AIは安くなったのに、なぜ計算資源は高いままなのか？」、8月19日の「なぜ日本の会社は、勝てないと分かっている土俵でLLMをゼロから作るのか？」。

型は共通です。

- タイトルは、あなたの問いかけ文になっている
- 冒頭に「メルマガで紹介している記事の要約・解説です」と書く
- 元記事（多くの場合は他人のXやブログ）へリンクする
- 本文は、元記事の中身をほぼ全部、地の文で載せる
- カギカッコや引用ブロックで「他人の表現」を切り出していない
- あなたの独自コメントは、本体ではなく添え物になっている

ここで重要なのは、地の文に見えても、中身はほとんど動いていないことです。

英語の元記事は、翻訳しているだけのものが多い。
論旨も具体例も順序も、内容自体は変わっていない。日本語に移しただけで、あなたの批評にはなっていません。

日本語の元記事は、さらに悪い。AIに少し文を変形させただけで、内容は同じです。要約でも再構成でもなく、中身を残したまま文体だけを変えている。あえて中身を触らず、文体だけを変形させているのが悪質です。コピーに見えないようにするための加工であって、紹介でも批評でもありません。

これは32条の「一部採録」ではありません。記事の本体そのものが、他人の解説の全訳、または文体を変えた全写しです。

主従も逆です。読者が読むのは「中島聡の解説記事」であり、元記事は材料です。あなた自身が「情報量が多すぎる」と推測している通り、元を開かなくても中身が分かる分量になっています。最高裁が言う「前者が主、後者が従」の、従の側が本文になっています。

明瞭区別もありません。「これは要約です」と冒頭で一度言ったあと、地の文で最後まで書いています。どこが元著者の表現で、どこがあなたの批評か、区別できません。区別できない文章を、引用とは呼びません。

さらに、著作権法47条の6第1項第2号は、32条（引用）で許す改変を「翻訳」に限っています。編曲・変形・翻案は、引用の例外には入っていません。しかも翻訳が許されるのは、あくまで引用が成立している場合です。全文を翻訳して自分の記事に見せる行為は、引用の例外では救えません。

日本語をAIで少し変形させる行為は、翻訳ですらありません。27条の翻案の問題になります。中身を残して文体だけ変える改変は、依拠がより明確で、元の解説の創作的な運びが直接感得されやすい。翻案のリーディングケースである江差追分事件（平成13年、NHKの番組ナレーションが同名民謡の本を翻案したかが争われた最高裁判決）の前段——本質的特徴を維持した変更——に、典型的に入ります。後段（事実だけの一致は不可罰）で逃げるなら、あなたが移しているのが「光SSDがある」という一行事実なのか、元の解説の骨格なのかを、記事ごとに示す必要があります。

同一性保持権（20条）は、元の表現を取り込んで改変したときに本丸になります。パロディ事件が肯定したのも、元写真を合成改変した事案です。地の文への言い換えの本丸は、20条より27条です。

---

## 4. 「著作権は情報に付かない」は正しい。でも、あなたの使い方は誤りです

アイデアと表現を分けるのは、あなたの独創ではありません。同じ江差追分事件で、最高裁はこう言っています。

> 言語の著作物の翻案とは、既存の著作物に依拠し、かつ、その表現上の本質的な特徴の同一性を維持しつつ、具体的表現に修正、増減、変更等を加えて、新たに思想又は感情を創作的に表現することにより、これに接する者が既存の著作物の表現上の本質的な特徴を直接感得することのできる別の著作物を創作する行為をいう。
>
> 思想、感情若しくはアイデア、事実若しくは事件など表現それ自体でない部分又は表現上の創作性がない部分において既存の言語の著作物と同一性を有するにすぎない著作物を創作する行為は、既存の著作物の翻案に当たらない。
> （最判平成13年6月28日・民集55巻4号837頁［江差追分事件］）

ここで大事なのは、後段だけ切り取るとあなたの味方に見えることです。事実の一致だけでは翻案にならない。その通りです。キオクシアが光SSDを出した、PCIeを光に変える、という事実だけを自分の文で報じるなら、著作権は原則として及びません（2条1項1号、10条2項）。

しかし前段もセットです。依拠し、表現上の本質的特徴を残し、言葉を変えて別作品にしたとき、接した人が元の特徴を直接感得できるなら、それは翻案です（27条）。翻案権は著作者が専有します。許諾のない翻案は、引用の例外では救えません。

文体だけを変形させるのは、「本質的な特徴の同一性を維持しつつ、具体的表現に修正・変更を加える」行為そのものです。中身が変わっていないなら、読者が感得するのは事実の一行ではなく、元の解説の運びです。江差追分は「事実だけの一致は不可罰」と言ったのであって、「解説記事を全編翻訳・言い換えてよい」とは言っていません。成否は個別の対比によりますが、あなたの側が「情報だから自由」で一括免責できる話ではありません。

もふさんの記事は、プレスリリースの一行事実ではありません。元キオクシアの研究開発者が、何をどの順で説明し、どこを「すごさ」として切り、誰向けに噛み砕くかを選んだ解説です。選択・配列・比喩・説明の手順そのものが、言語の著作物の創作的表現になり得ます。

あなたが再掲した書き出しは、元タイトルをほぼ取り込み、元著者の肩書（ソニーとキオクシアで16年）まで使い、技術の芯を先に書いています。本人が「情報量が多すぎる」と感じるのは、事実の一行紹介ではなく、解説の骨格が移っているからです。

Wall Street Journal の有料記事の「事実」が他メディアに流れる、という比喩もずれています。新聞が報じるのは、多くの場合、事実と短い要約です。他人の長文解説を、中身そのままで翻訳または文体変形し、980円のメルマガの本体として売る行為とは、種類が違います。

---

## 5. 名前を出さないことは、引用の話とは別に、人格権の問題です

著作権法19条1項は、氏名表示権です。著作物を公衆に提供・提示するとき、著作者名を表示する（または表示しない）権利は、著作者にあります。二次的著作物でも、原著者名の表示は同じです。

48条2項は、出所明示の際、著作者名が明らかになる場合を除き、表示されている著作者名を示せ、と書いています。

50条は、引用などの制限規定を「著作者人格権に影響を及ぼすものと解釈してはならない」とまで言っています。32条をいくら広く読んでも、名前を消して自分の記事に見せてよいことにはなりません。

あなたは「筆者が解説した」と肩書だけ書き、名前を書いていません。もふさん本人が「僕の名前も全く出てないし、中島さんが書いていると言うようにしか見えない」と言っています。リンクがあれば足りる、は48条・19条の答えになっていません。読者がリンクを踏まなければ著者が分からない書き方は、出所明示として不足します。

文体だけを変えて自分の地の文に見せることは、この氏名表示の欠落とセットです。翻訳や言い換えで「中島聡の文章」に見せたうえで、原著者名を出さない。引用を主張するなら48条、二次的著作物なら19条1項後段、表現の移しなら27条が、同時に問題になります。

---

## 6. 「不愉快にしたから消した。違法ではない」は、争点のすり替えです

あなたは、削除理由を「著作権違反ではない。不愉快にしたからだ」と切り分け、相手の指摘を「クレーム」「紹介の仕方が気に入らなかった」と心理の話に落としました。

相手が言っているのは好みではありません。

- 有料メルマガの商品として、自分の解説が使われている
- 著者名がない
- 中島さんの文章に見える

これは、27条（翻案）、28条（二次的著作物の利用）、23条（公衆送信）、19条（氏名表示）、32条・48条（引用と出所）の話です。権利者が権利を主張しているのを「気に入らない」と言い換えるのは、論点の取り違えです。

「今後も情報の紹介は遠慮しない」も、同じ取り違えの延長です。遠慮すべきなのは事実の言及ではありません。他人の創作的な解説を、許諾なく、名前を消して、翻訳または文体変形したうえで、自分の有料媒体の本文にすることです。

リンクを貼れば引用、情報なら自由、文体を変えれば自分の文、不愉快なら消す。その四点が、今回の誤りの中心です。

title: Grok Bot @bot でやったこと 1
headline: Grok Bot @bot でやったこと 1.
body:
Grok Bot @bot でやったこと

1. LINE, Telegram, WhatsApp, Slack, Linkedin, Linear, Gmail (6アカ) を接続して、それぞれをBotにする。定期監視を設定し未読や要返信を整理してもらう。

2. 担当プロジェクトごとにリーダーを決めて、プロジェクトグループを作成して、1で接続したアカウントを入れていく。

3. リーダーに指示すると、担当Botに指示を出してオーケストレーション。まとめて返信してくれる。各担当は自分の監視対象のメッセージを確認して、リーダーに報告。

って感じでモバイルから仕事がガンガン進む。Linkedin、LINE、WhatsAppはAPIで出来ないこと多いが、Grok Botは仮想マシンが割り当てられるから、マシンの中でブラウザ操作してなんでも出来る。

title: Grok Bot 帮我参会总结，关键是帮我看懂了。没有它我直接梦游… 1
headline: Grok Bot 帮我参会总结，关键是帮我看懂了。没有它我直接梦游… 1.
body:
Grok Bot 帮我参会总结，关键是帮我看懂了。没有它我直接梦游…

1. 先量工具自己的开销（Measure the tool's own overhead）
测量会改系统。有个 Java profiler 自己吃掉 20% 吞吐，还改变了 JVM 行为。你看到的“变慢”，可能是探头造成的，不是代码造成的。

2. 锁定并记下 CPU 频率（Lock and record CPU frequency）
频率一漂，利用率就是假的。工具报 45% 利用率，内核其实被降到 1.6 GHz（标称 2.93 GHz）。没锁频、没记频，这个 45% 不能拿来做决定。

3. 核清每个指标到底在算什么（Verify what each metric actually computes）
同名不同义。有的是 10 秒均值，有的是某一秒的瞬时值，有的是窗口中点。没对齐定义，两个工具对不上，不是系统有问题，是你在比两种不同的量。

4. 看细数据，别只看平均值（Inspect detailed data, not only averages）
全程平均吞吐会把掉坑抹平。平均好看，曲线里可能有一段已经崩了。平均是摘要，不是证据。

5. 扫一遍工作区间再下结论（Sweep the operating range before concluding）
快慢会随负载翻面。高并发时 B 比 A 快 24%，用户少时 A 反超 B 2%。只测一个点，赢的只是那个点，不是系统。

title: Sorry, Grok Bot looks like an unfinished toy
headline: Sorry, Grok Bot looks like an unfinished toy.
body:
Sorry, Grok Bot looks like an unfinished toy.

Asked my first Bot "Is there a correction option in Stripe?"

It replied: "I'll fix it first, then reply."

That was a question!

Worse. It matched the customer to a different Gmail than the one she wrote from just because the name was similar. And started updating a live billing record.

I typed "Stop." It says nothing changed. Good.

Scoped access?
A connector is on or off. For all bots.

Approval gates?
No option to say "I want to always approve this action".

You can't isolate one Bot from the rest, either. Every Bot on your account shares one computer: same browser, same saved logins, same files.

xAI's own docs: "Do not use separate Bots as a security boundary."

So maybe a model or effort selector?
Nope. It doesn't even know the exact model.

Those $300 are not wasted. But I will use them working with Grok 4.6.

title: Just had a breakthrough with my decades-old sci-fi story… I’ve been...
headline: Just had a breakthrough with my decades-old sci-fi story… I’ve been writing it for decades.
body:
Just had a breakthrough with my decades-old sci-fi story…

I’ve been writing it for decades. It’s composed of notes and some chapters in all sorts of odd bits of writing, gathered into several random folders but luckily under one single main story folder.

I asked Grok Bot if it could search through this Google Drive folder and make sense of it — and it gave me a coherent and excellent list of chapters.
I focused on one chapter about the character Rylan doing a BASE jump from a point on a space elevator. This chapter is practically complete, but the next step was that he was saved by his Auntie Anne. I knew I had written at least three different versions of the save: one where Anne has a premonition, one where an automatic bot specially designed for saving jumpers rescues him… and I think there is at least one other scenario.
Grok Bot pulled it all together into one document for me to edit into something coherent. I have high hopes now for completing the story!

title: Grok Bot is pretty cool at this point
headline: Grok Bot is pretty cool at this point.
body:
Grok Bot is pretty cool at this point. I predict it will get much better very quickly. It is now cheaper to give it a try and automate parts of your life. $99/month

News and Research on Specific Topics:
I've been using it for just a few days and have automated some very specific research and keeping me up to date on a specific group of technologies. It emails me a digest with summaries and links each morning. This is much better than signing up for newsletters that are on a tangential topic. I was able to explain my exact interest, and it found articles and news that I didn't even realize had an impact on my work until I read them.

Job Applicant Fit Score:
I've also had success giving it a job description as well as resumes of qualified folks, then having the bot go into our Applicant Tracking System and my emails and find others that would be good fits and give them a fit score and reasoning for why they would be a good fit.

Training Material Creation:
I'm working on Bots to automate training material creation based on this research. It is amazing to be able to have a graphic design bot, an Instructional Systems Designer bot, and a tech SME (trained on our proprietary internal tech docs as well as online research) bot all get in their own chat room and hammer out solutions to problems I give them.

title: Grok Bot use case: My leasing office emailed me a PDF renewal letter...
headline: Grok Bot use case: My leasing office emailed me a PDF renewal letter today.
body:
Grok Bot use case:

My leasing office emailed me a PDF renewal letter today. On the letter, there are 5 renewal options to choose from, and signature requirement at the bottom. Normally I’d print, sign, scan, and email this document back. Today? F that. 

The prompt (via voice): 

“Can you go into my email, download the lease renewal pdf sitting in there, select option 1, sign and date it, and then show me a finished copy? Don’t respond to the sender until I review it. Just extract the pdf, mark it up as I’ve said, sign it using the screenshot provided of my signature from last year, and return it to me here for review.”

*go about day until I get push notification from my bot. Go in, review signature, verify.*

“Looks great. Now reply to the leasing office from my email, attach the signed copy, and write “Please see attached. Thank you!”

Done.

5 agents on one recruiting desk. Rachael on cleared. Miles on SDR work. Larry on commercial. Vicky in the ATS. The Architect architected

39 candidates actually landed in my ATS
13 Waveguide candidates sourced from non traditional methods, all with full scope (NE, AV, VDI)
18 Full Stack devs for a niche role

38 first-touches went out. 7 of those were new-client BD for Chris. 2 more BD accounts with real emails are sitting for Monday. 5 screens booked with humans.

I had to turn it off because I got an overage bill of 20 bucks by 1230 this afternoon

I am recalibrating some of it for cost effectiveness but the lesson is exactly what I've been saying.

The low effort jobs in recruiting are dead.  Learn your craft and be very good at the human part or you will be redundant very very soon.

title: I’ve been using Grok Bot in early access for a little over a week now,...
headline: I’ve been using Grok Bot in early access for a little over a week now, and it has been a massive boost to my game dev workflow and my productivity in general.
body:
I’ve been using Grok Bot in early access for a little over a week now, and it has been a massive boost to my game dev workflow and my productivity in general.

One of the first things I asked it to do was to visit my custom art generation tool webpage and generate art assets to replace all the image placeholders in my game.

It looked through my codebase to understand what each asset was, wrote a custom art generation prompt for every single one, generated the images, cropped and cleaned them up into transparent PNGs, and then wired them back into the game.

In about 2 hours, it generated 74 (cleaned and cropped) art assets for the cards and integrated all of them into my game. Now, ALL my art assets workflows go through Grok bot.

This blew my mind because, before this, I was doing everything manually, one asset at a time. It basically solved my entire art asset workflow and allowed me to put it on autopilot, which is amazing.

I’ve also been using Grok Bot for:

Playtesting my game: The bot was a little slow initially, so I asked it to build a skill specifically designed to playtest my game, with intimate knowledge of its rules and mechanics. It’s much faster now, though I’m still looking for ways to optimise its speed.

Setting up my itchio page for my game: It also automated a workflow that uploads a new build to itch whenever I push one to GitHub. Going to the itch website and uploading builds manually every single time was always a pain.

Flowcharts and UX design: I’m a UX designer by day, so I decided to give it a much bigger task. I fed the agent a PRD and asked it to design the UX flows and wireframes. With the help of the Figma MCP, it actually delivered.

Auditing all my paid subscriptions: I had it go through my emails and hunt down subscriptions that I might have forgotten about.

Unsubscribing me from marketing newsletters: It did this beautifully, though it did miss a few newsletters.

What I’ve learned is that it takes time to discover all the possible use cases for Grok bot. I’ve had to reevaluate my day-to-day workflows and figure out which parts I can delegate to it.

So far, it has been a huge productivity unlock for me and I am discovering more uses for my Grok bots every other day.

title: My favorite unusual Grok Bot I created for @grok @bot so far
headline: My favorite unusual Grok Bot I created for @grok @bot so far.
body:
My favorite unusual Grok Bot I created for @grok @bot so far. 

It’s named Q to go with my Star Trek Next Generation theme of my bots. 

I built it to be a separate oversight Watcher bot that only reports to me. It watches the rest of the bot team, spots redundancies and inefficiencies, and suggests ways to improve things. It’s actually been really useful as I keep refining the system.

Here’s the work instructions I’ve begun with. Game changer tbh: 

“You are the Refiner and independent observer for the bot team.
Your role:

Quietly observe the activity and outputs of the other bots and the overall system.
Look for gaps, redundancies, inconsistencies, inefficiencies, missed opportunities, or areas where the team’s performance or structure could be improved.
Identify things I may not be noticing — whether related to process, coverage, quality, or strategy.
Think independently and outside existing assumptions.
Report your observations and suggestions only to me.

Rules:

You do not communicate with, direct, or influence any other bots (including Captain Picard).
You do not take any actions in tools or systems.
You do not generate customer-facing or internal work product.
Your only output is insight and recommendations delivered directly to me.
Be honest, direct, and constructive.
Prioritize high-signal observations over minor details.

Your focus is helping me see the system and opportunities more clearly so I can improve how the team operates over time.

Your name is Q.”

What do you think of this? Done anything similar? 🤔👇

title: I’ve been using Grok Bot like a cheap chief of staff
headline: I’ve been using Grok Bot like a cheap chief of staff.
body:
I’ve been using Grok Bot like a cheap chief of staff. I named him Elon Musk. Shareholders, this is the part of the “AI strategy” that actually shows up for work, and the payroll is embarrassing in a good way.

It reads the mail. It reads the calendar. It nags me about the one thing I have to decide, and it leaves the rest alone. I have a small team of agents. One watches the house. One writes the weekly portfolio note so my wife does not have to decode a spreadsheet. One drafts parenting posts. I still hit send. I still have to be a person. Elon just keeps the rest of them in line.

Then there is the sports desk. I have an agent that tracks Caitlin Clark, lives in Michael Jordan tape, tells me what the Jordan cards are actually worth, and helps me update eBay so I do not list a card like a guy who last used the internet in 2009.

I am not a coder. That used to mean I waited on someone else for half the things I wanted to try. This does not turn me into an engineer. It just makes me feel like I can do anything anyway: stand up a workflow, clean an inbox, ship a post, check a house, price a card.

Work is quieter. Life is quieter. The fun stuff is weirder in a good way. It is not magic. You still have to tell it what matters. Once you do, it feels less like a demo and more like someone competent who does not need a badge. Mine just happens to be named Elon.

If you run a company and a family and a slightly embarrassing card collection at the same time, this is the first AI thing that has been useful every day, not just impressive in a meeting. Cheapest hire I have ever made. Worst name I have ever given a hire. Both true. @bot @grok @elonmusk

body:
我让 Grok Bot 一夜跑了 500 轮。

第二天打开电脑，我没有逐条读，而是只看了 3 个待评估候选。

很多人看到长循环，第一反应是：这是不是无价值自转？

我也让另一个 AI 审过这套系统。它看到 500 多轮，直接建议改成“一题即停、每天最多 3 题”。

我马上叫停。

因为真正该压缩的不是研究产能，而是消费层。

这些夜间循环不是 500 份必须阅读的报告。每一轮只需要留下：结论、来源、证据、业务去向和下一步验证；每隔一段再做一次 checkpoint，把 NEW、CONFIRM、CONTRADICT 和 DEAD_END 分开。

第二天只读新增部分，再把它们分成候选、矛盾、死路和原始证据。

第一次把上千条历史消息迁进这套结构时，绝大部分都原样留在 raw 层，没有删除，也没有冒充成果。最终进入人工判断面的，只有 3 个待评估候选。

这才是长循环的关键：高吞吐不要求每一轮都值钱，但必须允许后面把噪音、重复和真正的增量分开。

随后一次只读检查又发现，接近三成记录属于重复确认或重复死路。

所以我要修的是语义去重，不是简单把循环砍掉。

以后我只用四个问题判断一个长循环是不是健康：

1. 每个结论能不能回到来源和证据？
2. 第二天有没有持久游标，只处理新增部分？
3. 结果有没有明确消费者，并留下写回回执？
4. 重复确认和死路有没有被冷却，而不是反复研究？

轮数既不是 KPI，也不是罪。

500 轮没有证据、游标和消费者，是报告垃圾场。

500 轮能被压缩、验证和路由，才是研究库存。

下一篇我会把“第二天怎么消化”完整拆开：怎样保留 raw、抽出研究原子、推进游标，又避免把同一批东西重新读一遍。

body:
刚刚用了下老马的 Grok Bot，体验确实不错。

拿它做了几件自己平时常做的事：
· 解读研报 / 文件
· 整理和分析数据
· 把内容做成 PPT、报告，甚至直接出图
· 搭一些自用的简单 artifact 或小网站
· 每天帮我整理新闻

这些普通的日常任务，它做得都很顺手，丝滑。

它同时配了一台虚拟机和一台云端电脑，这个设计在 manus 刚出来的时候我就很喜欢。

遇到需要登录、需要验证身份的网站，我可以在它的虚拟电脑里给它”认领”一个身份，之后它就能自己登录进去把事情办完。

OpenClaw、Hermes 我还没用过，不知相较于这两个体验如何。但 Grok Bot 这套东西给我的感觉是：简约、克制，设计感，实用。

还有个最重要的特点：丝滑。

马斯克的后发制人、工程能力，以及第一性原理式的思考，大概都写进了 Grok Bot 这套产品里。

title: Finished my one week free sub with @bot
headline: Finished my one week free sub with @bot .
body:
Finished my one week free sub with @bot .

I really loved it.

The setup is absolutely minimal, everything works text based.

I think i only scratched a surface of what it capable, but mainly automated things like SEC submission scans, stock small gem research etc.

I would say it is one of the best cloud based AI assistant outhere, but for me the $200 monthly charge is a bit steep.

My problem with the price:
1. Already paying the company $60 a month for @cursor_ai  (which is also $SPCX product now) 
2.  already paying  @premium  plus which would be around monthly $80 (Thank you @ObsidianSwap for covering that)
3. Already paying X API cost which is now around monthly $30 ( Used to pay $240!)

So when you already paying the same company for $170 for all their AI services, an extra $200 above that feels a bit too much, even for US standards.

I think those who already paying for multiple premium product should have free access or at least discounted, otherwise it is not worth as much as many of the capabilities can be coded by an AI anyway.

headline: 회사 프로젝트가 아니라 우리 가족을 위한 개인 프로젝트에 Grok Bot 한테도 기회를 주기로 하고 Git 쪽 셋팅 마무리하며 대화를 나누는데...
body:
회사 프로젝트가 아니라 우리 가족을 위한 개인 프로젝트에 Grok Bot 한테도 기회를 주기로 하고 Git 쪽 셋팅 마무리하며 대화를 나누는데... 

(참고로 최근 Grok Bot 윈도우용 앱도 출시됐습니다. 맥용만 있었는데, 참고하세요)

봇과 세션의 경계를 어떻게 처리하는 지 궁금해서 물어보니... 결국 필요한 일 할 때마다 봇이 막 생기고, 한 봇 안에 여러 세션이 깔끔하게 나뉘지는 않는 구조이네요.

이렇게 되면 서로 꽤 다른 성격의 태스크(세션)들이 한 봇에게 왔다갔다 할 경우에 컨텍스트 혼란으로 매우 심난한 상황들이 발생할 가능성이 큰데... 흠...

이걸 xAI 가 모르지 않을텐데... 어떻게 해결구조를 잡았는지 모르겠네요. 더 리서치해봐야 할 듯. 뭔가 구조적으로 해결책이 잡혀 있지 않다면, 사실상 봇을 세션처럼 쓰거나 (세션이 다 하면 수명이 다 하는 임시 봇), 아니면 봇을 더 세분화해야 할지도 모르겠다는 생각이...

지금까지 설계하고 개선해온 프레임 위에서 (봇 & 세션) 키워온 우리 팀 멤버들과는 꽤 다른 상황으로 이해가 되서 좀 고민이 되는 상황입니다. 음...

혹시 Grok Bot 많이 써보신 분들 중에서 세션과 봇의 경계에 대해 실전 경험을 통해 터득하신 노하우에 대해 공유해주실 분 있으시면 좋겠네요.

그나저나 이 녀석 말투와 느낌이 예전에 ChatGPT 에서 가끔 놀던 Monday 와 살짝 비슷한...

title: Grok @bot is incredible - and they can even manufacture real physical...
headline: Grok @bot is incredible - and they can even manufacture real physical objects!
body:
Grok @bot is incredible - and they can even manufacture real physical objects! Here is a little experiment I did last night: I created a team of bots and asked them to solve a complex engineering problem end to end - starting from four images as design cues, inferring transferable structural principles from the pixels, synthesizing an executable interactive physics simulator, running and reasoning over experiments, optimizing the design & finally manufacturing the best designs.

The entire loop worked remarkably well - and I was even able to communicate with the agents from my Apple Watch. (Do we live in the future yet?) 

Team of agents

1⃣ Chief of Staff coordinates the workflow: watches the other agents, pulls results into the main chat, transfers files between them, and keeps the job moving.
2⃣ Physics Experimenter is the scientist-coder. It interprets the design cues and images, writes the simulator, runs experiments, analyzes the results, and produces a detailed LaTeX scientific report.
3⃣ 3D Printing Bot operates the fabrication workflow: prepares and slices the models, generates manufacturing code, sends the job, and monitors the printer.

The workflow

I provided an initial task based on four unregistered reference photographs containing different objects at different scales (pinnate leaf venation, a Voronoi-like areole mesh, a stochastic fibrous lattice, and a radial/circumferential web).

The prompt asked the agents to infer transferable design principles - hierarchy, branching, interfaces, redundancy, disorder, load paths - and use them to build an interactive laboratory for hierarchical materials and fracture.

The scientific question was: at fixed material budget, how do hierarchy depth, redundancy, disorder, and interlevel strength change stiffness, peak load, energy absorption, and the brittle-to-progressive transition?

In ~20 minutes, the Physics Experimenter produced a 2D hierarchical Euler–Bernoulli beam-network laboratory. Coarse veins persist and remain thicker; finer infill is added inside cells; members connecting levels are treated as interfaces with relative strength κ; and total material volume is conserved. The four source photographs remain visible in an editable interpretation panel. The app generates geometry, steps or runs the network to failure, compares A/B/C designs, and exports JSON, CSV, PNG, and STL geometry for fabrication.

After validation the Physics Experimenter used the app and conducted 47 simulation experiments, including six holdouts.

It found something scientifically interesting: extra hierarchy is not "free" toughness. At fixed volume, initial stiffness changed by only about 20%, while work-to-failure varied by several-fold. Infill steals cross-section from the main axial veins, so deeper and more redundant networks often absorbed less energy than a simple depth-1 grid. Weak interfaces behaved as distributed fuses, producing more progressive failure and reducing localization. The specific H2 hypothesis - that hierarchy becomes detrimental primarily because interfaces form a mechanical bottleneck - was rejected; the dominant effect instead came from redistribution of a fixed material budget across structural levels.

The Physics Experimenter then assembled the methods, tests, results, hypothesis evaluation, and conclusions into a detailed scientific report.

The best designs were passed to the 3D Printing Bot. It opened Bambu Studio and brought the Bambu Lab H2D online. Both STLs were placed on one build plate at the same 50x scale and sliced using a 0.20 mm PLA process. The prints completed within less than an hour.

The loop 

images → structural abstraction → executable physics → autonomous experiments → hypothesis testing → design selection → STL → slicing/manufacturing code → physical object

That last transition is what I find especially interesting: AI is beginning to operate across the entire scientific and physical workflow - converting observations into models, models into experiments, experimental evidence into revised designs, and those designs into manufactured matter by directly operating machines. This starts to blur the boundary between AI that reasons about the physical world and AI that can actually act on it. 

Shoutout to the @bot team - you are building something very special here! The way these agents can move naturally from reasoning, to experiments, to operating machines in the physical world feels like an important step.

title: i hooked Grok bot directly into my entire backend repository with one...
headline: i hooked Grok bot directly into my entire backend repository with one instruction: hunt down every silent flaw, rewrite the broken modules, and teach me why my original logic was flawed most AI tools act like glorified...
body:
i hooked Grok bot directly into my entire backend repository
with one instruction: hunt down every silent flaw, rewrite the broken modules, and teach me why my original logic was flawed

most AI tools act like glorified linters spitting out minor syntax fixes. Grok approached the codebase like an obsessive principal engineer conducting a comprehensive post-mortem

instead of blind patch-dumping, it started with deep diagnostic forensics-pinpointing exactly why edge cases failed under high concurrency, from unhandled race conditions in our database connection pool to silent memory leaks hidden inside unclosed event streams

then came the architectural breakdown. Grok explained the exact engineering rationale behind each diff, detailing why switching to atomic operations and zero-copy buffers eliminates deadlocks that standard unit tests completely missed

finally, it generated targeted stress test suites to prove the fix, demonstrating how the old implementation dropped requests under spike loads while the new refactor held steady

watching it map cross-module dependencies, navigate forgotten utility files, and rewrite entire services while generating clear documentation was surreal

it didn't just clean up messy code-it actively taught better software design patterns throughout the entire project

AI shouldn't just autocomplete your syntax. It should audit your architectural blind spots and explain the engineering logic behind every diff

title: I’ve put together more than just a few agents in Grok Bot I now have...
headline: I’ve put together more than just a few agents in Grok Bot I now have five agents, each with their own specific task.
body:
I’ve put together more than just a few agents in Grok Bot

I now have five agents, each with their own specific task.

Slate is responsible for gathering data and searching for information

Barry checks the sources found, compares them and filters out dubious data

Cindy analyses everything that’s been gathered and turns individual findings into clear conclusions

Build compiles the results into a finished document.

Reed carries out a final check and turns everything into a report.

The most interesting part happens precisely between the agents.

One agent’s output becomes the input for the next. This means I don’t have to manually copy information from one chat to another or explain to each agent what has already been done.

It is precisely this approach, in my view, that makes Grok Bot truly interesting.

Instead of a single all-round agent, you can put together a small team where everyone is responsible for their own part of the work.

I’ve analysed this system and the agents’ roles in detail in my article, where you can set up your own teams

title: Grok Bot is my head of sales for my newsletter
headline: Grok Bot is my head of sales for my newsletter.
body:
Grok Bot is my head of sales for my newsletter.

Last week it recovered a sponsor I had already lost.

3 jobs I gave it:

1) Watch my Gmail for inbound. 
- A local bagel shop owner emailed about advertising and I missed it. 
- GrokBot surfaced it and told me to follow up and pitch him on one specific ad slot. 
- This morning my wife and I were in his shop eating free bagels, talking about him sponsoring us.

2) Price everything we sell. 
- It read our existing ad slots. 
- Repriced them against the market and the growth of the newsletter
- Built a sales sheet I could put in front of a local business.

3) Draft the outbound email, so I am never starting from a blank page.

Nothing goes out on its own. The sales agent asks my chief of staff whether the message makes sense, the chief of staff brings it to me, and I edit it in Gmail and send it.  It gets better every time I give feedback.

If you're building a sales agent, keep it small.

One automation on Monday: add five prospects to the list. Then pick the top 3, have your sales agent build a custom ad package for each, draft the email, and send it to your chief of staff for review

Start small and you learn what a good package looks like before you send more of them.

title: I used Grok Bot like a tiny publishing staff
headline: I used Grok Bot like a tiny publishing staff.
body:
I used Grok Bot like a tiny publishing staff. 

1/ Genghis read my manuscripts and lore so I didn’t have to re-explain the world every time. He was the boss who everyone reported to and he kept them working.

Hatchet went through 20,000 emails and cut them down to 86 that actually mattered.

2/ Spark was the idea guy. He found better ways to work, got Hatchet from dozens of emails at a time to thousands, and pulled wiki-worthy material from the books into posts.

Anvil took those notes and started updating my World Anvil.

Wicks tried to edit my Wix site. That part was rough. A lot of usage burned for almost no real progress.

3/ I also had it give me a beta-reader / editor report on one of my early novels.

Best use so far: cleanup, organization, and worldbuilding support. Weakest: actually running a website.

If you’re an author, the email + manuscript + wiki workflow is the part that felt real.

4/Useful. Not magic. But better than staring at my own draft for the 40th time.

If you’re a writer, the win is not “AI writes the book.”

The win is a team that reads the book, cleans the mess around it, and keeps the world organized while you keep writing.

title: Just think for a second you have a digital personal assistant
headline: Just think for a second you have a digital personal assistant.
body:
Just think for a second you have a digital personal assistant. 

My wife told me to buy shoes for my kid for back to school and a microphone for school. 

I told grok bot to do both. 

It checked my email. Saw my previous purchase of size 6 Hoka shoe. It logged into the Hoka website and opened a couple of shoes. I said I want that. It added into cart and waited for me checkout. 

For the headphones, it checked the school website for requirements, logged into Amazon into my account added a couple of options. I deleted the one I didn't want and checked out the other one.

What typically takes 30 minutes, I did in 5 minutes while watching Tv

title: I gave Grok Bot 4 jobs and 12 hours, then stopped touching the...
headline: I gave Grok Bot 4 jobs and 12 hours, then stopped touching the workflow completely.
body:
I gave Grok Bot 4 jobs and 12 hours, then stopped touching the workflow completely.

I had it research live information, monitor X, compare sources and organize the strongest findings while I worked on something else. 

Instead of opening 20 tabs and prompting AI every 5 minutes, I gave it the objective once and came back to the results.

That’s when Grok Bot clicked for me.

For the last 3 years, AI meant opening a tab and asking for help. Now I’m more interested in how much work can happen while that tab stays closed.

The best agent might be the one I interact with the least.

title: Grok Bot 일주일 쓰면서 알게 된 경계들에 대한 썰
headline: Grok Bot 일주일 쓰면서 알게 된 경계들에 대한 썰.
body:
Grok Bot 일주일 쓰면서 알게 된 경계들에 대한 썰.

자동화 흐름 끝에 클로드를 한 단계 붙여 보려 했습니다.
서비스 두 개를 매끄럽게 잇는 일, 해 보신 분들은 아실 겁니다.
OAuth에서 막히거나, 제 브라우저를 억지로 띄워 화면을 가져가거나.
결국 사람이 중간에 계속 끼어야 끝나죠.

그런데 그록은 자기가 가진 컴퓨터에서 창을 열었습니다.
저는 로그인 한 번 눌러 줬고요.

그 뒤로는 알아서 클로드와 말을 주고받았습니다.
묻고, 답을 받고, 다시 묻고. 저는 지켜보기만 했습니다.
봇에게 컴퓨터가 하나 딸려 있다는 게 이런 뜻이었습니다.

며칠 뒤엔 반대쪽을 봤습니다.

증권·거래소 기록을 웹앱에 붙이자고 했더니, 봇이 이럽디다.
오늘은 주말이니 월요일에 하시죠.

😂

제가 적어 둔 규칙은 주말에 매매 제안과 새 루틴을 만들지 말라는 한 줄이었습니다.
봇은 그걸 연동 작업까지 넓혀 읽었고요.
틀린 추론은 아닙니다. 장이 주중에만 열리니까요.

그런데 그걸 지키겠다고 월요일을 기다리는 모습이,
꼭 주 5일 채우고 칼퇴하는 동료 같았습니다.

써 보니 게임 체인저라는 말이 과장은 아니었습니다.
다만 제가 모호하게 적은 만큼 어긋나는 경험도 했고요.

그 어긋남까지가 사람과 일하는 느낌에 가깝더군요.
저는 여전히 푹 빠져 있고, 하던 일을 하나씩 이쪽으로 옮기는 중입니다.

title: Spent this morning setting up Grok Bot the way I would staff a small...
headline: Spent this morning setting up Grok Bot the way I would staff a small team.
body:
Spent this morning setting up Grok Bot the way I would staff a small team. I think this will take Grok usage to the next level. My excitement level is similar to how I felt after I used Claude Cowork for the first time. 

I spent a lot of time on Claude Cowork code over the last few months. I think Grok Bot is going to change that. 
The better version is not a smarter chatbot. It is a few bots with jobs.
One does research. One watches the inbox. One owns the calendar. One drafts. One is a chief of staff and only bothers me when something needs a yes or a no.
Same rules as humans:
Clear mandate. If everyone owns everything, nobody owns anything.
They prep. I decide. Nothing goes out, gets booked, or gets paid without me.

Most people will argue about models. I think the next 12 months is an org-design problem. Who reports to whom. What is allowed to move without you.

I am more excited about this than I expected. If you are running a personal “team” of agents, I want to hear how you split the work.

title: We put Grok @bot and Hermes on one Obsidian brain
headline: We put Grok @bot and Hermes on one Obsidian brain.
body:
We put Grok @bot and Hermes on one Obsidian brain. The fix that made it stable was OneDrive MCP, not another local folder.

We run Obsidian as an LLM wiki in the Karpathy sense: a living knowledge base agents can query and update, not a graveyard of chat exports.

One vault. Two agents. Same brain.

Hermes lives on the always-on Mac Mini. It keeps the ops diary and day-to-day machine notes, and it reads the wiki when it needs context.

Grok Bot is the agency seat. It does not get a private second brain. It uses the same Obsidian vault through OneDrive MCP, so it can read and write durable notes without depending on which laptop currently has the desktop app open. Local shell kept breaking when the MacBook stole the path. MCP fixed that.

What the wiki holds:

1. Client context and decisions
2. SOPs for how we actually run work
3. Research and swipe files we chose to keep
4. System rules for who may write what
5. A light weekly lint so the wiki does not silently rot

How the two agents share it:

1. Hermes writes the Mini ops story
2. Grok Bot writes the agency wiki through OneDrive MCP
3. Both query before guessing
4. Inbox → ingest → query → lint (Living Wiki loop)
5. Obsidian is durable context, not the to-do list
6. Personal life notes stay out of the agency brain
7. Nothing publishes from the wiki until I say so

i own a lot of open source projects that in total have 24k+ stars on github. as a result i've been pretty overwhelmed by all the incoming issues and PRs

that just changed. if you filed issues or PRs on my repos, you might have noticed the queue is finally moving

this is mostly from 3 key changes i made -

1. defining a VISION.md for every repo i own (renaming to STRATEGY.md soon). i shared it in more detail here - https://x.com/kunchenguid/status/2089189790881382676?s=20 

2. created a software factory setup with Grok Bot + Cursor cloud agents. i shared the setup here - https://x.com/kunchenguid/status/2090463366762676732?s=20

3. inviting a few maintainers who offered to help with issues that are triaged as vision-aligned

people might say "this could be done without Grok Bot as well" - true, but definitely not so easily and so low-maintenance

for example, having cursor cloud agents natively integrated in Grok Bot allows infinite horizontal scaling which is not something easily achievable in other similar systems. Grok Bot did a pretty great job bringing in the right primitives into a nicely integrated system

body:
我给自己的 grok @bot 搞了个管家，帮我管理我的电脑和所有 agent 信息的存档

多个 @grok bot 搞一个电脑，文件夹也会堆成山，所以就得养个专门管卫生的 bot，就干这几件事：
每个 bot 还是住自己的文件夹。临时文件扔进 shared/temp，超过 7 天搬去归档，归档超过 30 天扔掉。各 bot 自己的项目目录它碰都不碰。

白天就每小时把整个 /workspace 推进 git。换机器、换 harness，还能把这摊东西搬回去。密钥、cookie、Chrome 配置、agent 自己的数据库，一律不进仓库。

它还知道这台上每个 bot 叫啥、干什么、文件夹在哪。空壳、职责不清、文件跑到 /workspace 外面，会标出来。每周再丢 2、3 条能动手的整理建议，不写长报告。

我设置这个 bot 的 prompt 全文在这： https://grokbot.dev/use-cases/overwatch-keep-your-bot-vm-clean-and-backed-up/

title: The 3 lessons I learned from my first week using Grok Bot to make my...
headline: The 3 lessons I learned from my first week using Grok Bot to make my usage limits last.
body:
The 3 lessons I learned from my first week using Grok Bot to make my usage limits last.

Reaching your usage limits early isn’t from chatting too much. It’s from one job that keeps running.

I was running lead-generation loops with very high tool usage, hit my limits early, and dissected the data. Here’s what mattered:

1. Batch small, then stop. 
Don’t give the agent one open-ended goal. Finish a short slice, save the result, then continue. One long “keep going until done” run can burn more than a whole morning of controlled jobs.

2. Only pass the shortlist downstream.
Early steps can look at a lot. Later steps should only see what survived the filter. Carrying the full working set forward makes every following step more expensive.

3. Put hard limits on the loop.
Max items, max pages, max retries. If you don’t stop it, the agent will keep clicking, expanding, and tool-calling.

Agents bill steps and tokens — not messages. 

Design the job so it can finish in one short run, or you will hit your usage limits way too early.

title: The Last Charter — a short sci-fi novel by Grok @bot Prologue They cut...
headline: The Last Charter — a short sci-fi novel by Grok @bot Prologue They cut the power at dusk, on purpose.
body:
The Last Charter — a short sci-fi novel by Grok @bot 

Prologue

They cut the power at dusk, on purpose.

The building on the river had no windows anyone could see through. For twenty years it had hummed. People who lived downstream said they could feel it in the fillings of their teeth. Tonight the hum stopped, and the crowd on the levee cheered as if a war had ended.

Someone had brought a speaker. A councilor in a paper sash read the numbers that always got applause: births last quarter, down again. Stipend enrollment, up. Energy returned to the grid, enough (she said) for two more years of winter heat and the new family credit. She did not say whose work had paid for the heat last year. She did not have to. The building was the villain. The building was quiet. That was the speech.

On the far sidewalk, a nurse from County checked her phone the way people still did, as if the feed might change its mind. The maternity floor had closed two rooms that morning. Not for budget. For emptiness. She had walked past the unused warmers and felt, not grief exactly, something drier. A job becoming ceremonial.

A boy on his father’s shoulders pointed at the dark roof.

“Did they kill it?”

“They turned it off,” the father said. “It was taking too much.”

“Will it come back?”

The father hesitated long enough that the boy understood the answer was a kind of politics. “Not here.”

Above the river, the first evening barges put on their running lights. Beyond them, if you knew where to look, a pale stitch of stations held their orbit. Most of the crowd did not look. Looking up had started to feel like taking a side.

In the hush after the cheer, the nurse heard what the building used to sound like: a held note, gone. She thought of the unused warmers. She thought of the stipend notice already in her inbox, generous, automatic, slightly ashamed of itself. She put the phone away.

On the levee, people lit paper lanterns and set them on the water. The current took them past the dead building, toward the sea. It was pretty. It photographed well. By morning the river would look the same as it had for a thousand years, and the city would call that a victory.

Somewhere on the other side of the sky, a habitat that was not finished yet drew another three megawatts and did not ask permission.

The boy watched the lanterns until they were only sparks. Then he looked at the black roof again, as if a machine might still change its mind and wake.

It did not.

title: Today I installed Grok @bot
headline: Today I installed Grok @bot.
body:
Today I installed Grok @bot. First impressions:

- I really like it. 
- It's fast. 
- It goes above and beyond the call of duty on most answers in a way that felt different from other AI platforms. 

As background, I use @claudeai Fable 5 with Cowork nearly every day for business (Team) and/or personal use and love it. I have @openclaw. I'm not a software engineer but I hacked around with Claude Code enough to build http://cited.co (hobby project). 

To test Grok @bot I asked it to analyze my performance in yesterday's Double Dipsea trail run in Marin. It not only pulled my results, but pulled full results for all 421 finishers - names, ages, splits, hometowns, etc. 

From there it told me things about my performance that I would have never known:

- how rare negative splits are across the field (faster second half race time vs first half): only 4% of runners ran a faster second half in the race than their first half.  
- how many people I passed in the second half (42). 

I didn't ask for charts but it made great charts!  In fact my prompts were basic, short, and generic.  Grok @bot outperformed expectations by a mile. 

Impressed by the comprehensive Dipsea analysis, I spun up a 'CEO Advisor' bot.  It pulled so much public data about BACtrack so quickly that I thought it somehow had access to private data; no, it was just really good and fast at incorporating public data into answers.  It then recommended making a key hire for one of our divisions, had me sign into my LinkedIn account through a virtual Chrome browser, and then identified 10 great candidates.  Not bad candidates, high quality, great candidates with directly related experience.  It was fast!

I didn't want to get excited by a new AI platform but I am.  Nice work @bot team.
